Title: Adjustments of Socially Vulnerable Populations in Galveston County, Texas USA Following Hurricane Ike
Chunks: 10,11,12,13,14,35,36,37,38,39
## 3. Study Area
Our study area covers Galveston County, located on the upper Texas Gulf Coast about 25 miles south of Houston. It is a large metropolitan area encompassing the Galveston Bay, East Bay, and West Bay (see Figure 1). The South Eastern Gulf of Mexico is one of the most Hurricane- and flood-prone areas in the United States, and on average experiences a major Hurricane once every 15 years [71]. Due to rising sea levels, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicts that the frequency of surge events in this region may increase dramatically and could become as frequent 200 days a year, with 80 to 100% attributed to higher tides [72].
**Figure 1.** Study Area (Galveston County). Notes: The figure outlines the location of Galveston County in the state of Texas, USA. Datum: NAD 1983, Projection/Coordinate System: UTM Zone 14N.
A large portion of Galveston County is Galveston Island, a low lying micro tidal barrier island. One of the unique features of Galveston Island is the seawall built in response to the 1900 storm, the deadliest ever recorded Hurricane in U.S. history, responsible for approximately 8000 fatalities. Despite significant structural mitigation efforts, (Other large infrastructure project targeting flood mitigation in the Galveston County include a large levee system in Texas city, built in response to Hurricane Carla in 1961 to protect some of the valuable industrial assets such oil refineries.) this area continues to be overwhelmed by coastal storms and hurricanes. Hurricane Ike (2008) was a recent category 2 storm that brought a surge level comparable to a category 5 hurricane and caused massive property damage [73,74]. In this research we focus on the impacts of Hurricane Ike, as it gives enough time post-2008 to explore the long-term responses of vulnerable populations to its catastrophic devastation.

## 4. Data
Data for this study came from various sources including the American Community Survey of U.S. Census Bureau, The Harris County Flood Control District, and The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Socio-economic and demographic block group level data for Galveston County for the years 2000 and 2015 were drawn from the Census American Community Survey [75,76]. We specifically focus on variables measuring various attributes of social vulnerability. These include the race and ethnicity, people in poverty, female population, female-headed households, number of renters, population with no vehicle, population under 5 years old and 65 years and older, unemployed population, number receiving social security income, number of population without a high school diploma, and population living in mobile homes. The population counts were converted into percentages, and the changes in percentages over the two periods were calculated at a block group level. There were changes in block group lines from 2000 to 2015. Specifically, there were 211 block groups in 2000 and only 194 block groups in 2015. Only block groups that were matched between the two periods were considered for analysis (n = 152). These data were chosen based on the “Social Vulnerability Concepts and Metrics” Table 1 in Cutter et al. (2003, pp. 246–249) [20]. Appendix ATable A3 shows the concept and the variable used to measure various concepts. While there are many other factors that contribute to a person or households’ vulnerability (e.g., Rural/Urban, Special Needs Populations), the data measuring them were not readily available at the block group level for both years.
**Table 1.** Summary Statistics of Variables that Capture Social Vulnerability.

## 4. Data
Hurricane Ike’s inundation level data were obtained from The Harris County Flood Control District [77]. The data were spatially joined with the Block group shapefile in order to analyze average inundation levels by block group. Five levels of inundation were created, including (1) less than 2 ft; (2) 2–4 ft; (3) 4–6 ft; (4) 6–8 ft; and (5) 8–10 ft. Categorizing inundation at different levels is intended to capture the varying degrees of damage on changes in socio-economic characteristics of households across block groups and over-time.
Flood zone areas were drawn from the FEMA [78]. Flood zone data was spatially joined with block group data, and the percentage areas for each of the flood zone classes were calculated for each block group. For this research, three different flood risk zones were used: A-zones, X-zones, and V-zones. A-zones represent areas with a 1% annual chance of flooding in the 100-year flood plain, V-zones represent coastal areas in the 100-year flood plain with a 1% annual chance of flooding and coastal velocity hazard, and X-zones represent moderate to low risk areas outside of the 1% and 0.2% chance of annual flooding outside of the 500 year floodplain [78]. Flood zones in the model capture the existing “objective” risk for flooding.
The summary statistics for model variables are reported in Table 1. Appendix ATable A1 and Table A2 report summary statistics of level variables corresponding to years 2000 and 2015, respectively.

## 5. Methods
### 5.1. Principal Component Analysis
To construct social vulnerability indices for each block group, principal component analysis (PCA) was employed. PCA extracts the dominant patterns within a data matrix to create a smaller set of uncorrelated components [79]. To retain the most influential components which described most of the variance within the data, the components were retained based on the Kaiser criterion, i.e., components for which eigen values were greater than or equal to 1.
The variables used in the construction of the Social Vulnerability index (SV) included block group level percentages for female population, female-headed households, renters, population with no vehicle, population under 5 years old, population 65 and older, unemployed population, population receiving social security income, percent with less than a high school degree, and percentage of the population living in mobile homes. Once the components were identified using PCA for each year, the unweighted average of the components was taken to create an SV index where each factor was assumed to have the same contribution to the block group’s overall social vulnerability. Positive values of SV indicate higher levels and negative values indicate lower levels of social vulnerability, respectively. Following the approach described in Cutter and Finch (2008), for the social vulnerability indices to be compared between the two years, they were transformed into z-scores [80].

#### Notes:
Data obtained from ACS Demographic and Housing Estimates, table DP05.
Multiyear estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS) are "period" estimates derived from a data sample collected over a period of time, as opposed to "point-in-time" estimates such as those from past decennial censuses. ACS 5-year estimate includes data collected over a 60-month period. The date of the data is the end of the 5-year period. For example, a value dated 2014 represents data from 2010 to 2014. However, they do not describe any specific day, month, or year within that time period.
Multiyear estimates require some considerations that single-year estimates do not. For example, multiyear estimates released in consecutive years consist mostly of overlapping years and shared data. The 2010-2014 ACS 5-year estimates share sample data from 2011 through 2014 with the 2011-2015 ACS 5-year estimates. Because of this overlap, users should use extreme caution in making comparisons with consecutive years of multiyear estimates.
Please see "Section 3: Understanding and Using ACS Single-Year and Multiyear Estimates" on publication page 13 (file page 19) of the 2018 ACS General Handbook for a more thorough clarification.

# City of League City, Texas


# Section 108 Loan Pre -Application for the


# Main Street/Park Avenue CDBG Neighborhood


# Introduction
The City of League City, Texas is requesting $1,591,860 in funding under the Section 108 Loan Guarantee
Program of the U.S. Departme nt of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development
Block Grant (CDBG) Program. The Section 108 Loan Guarantee Program allows CDBG Entitlement
Jurisdictions to pledge up to five years of expected CDBG funding to guarantee a loan as a source of
financing for economic development, housing rehabilitation, public facilities, and infrastructure. Cities
such as League City do not receive enough CDBG funding in any one year to allow for the completion of
large -scale physical development and rehabil itation projects. In addition, HUD regulations to not allow
Entitlement Jurisdictions to “stock -pile” their allocations over several years to build sufficient funding for
a project. Therefore, the loan guarantee program provides loans large enough to car ry out larger local
projects that can revitalize and improve neighborhoods. The loans are required to be repaid within 20 years
and to not absorb all of the annual CDBG allocation. The current and future CDBG allocations are a
security for the loan.
Se ction 108 obligations are financed through underwritten public offerings. Financing between public
offerings is provided through an interim lending facility established by HUD. Interest rates on interim
borrowing are priced at the 3 -month London Interban k Offered Rate (LIBOR) plus 20 basis points (0.2%).
As of August 16, 2016, the 3 -month LIBOR rate is 0.82%, and with the added 0.2%, the total is 1.02%.
Permanent financing is tied to yields on the U.S. Treasury securities of similar maturity to the prin cipal
amount. A small additional spread, depending on maturity, will be added to the Treasury market yield to
determine the actual interest rate.
The activities to be carried out with the Section 108 -guaranteed loan must meet HUD’s community
development objectives as well as the City’s priorities detailed in its latest PY 2017 -2021 Consolidated
Plan. The primary objective of the CDBG program and the Section 108 -guaranteed loan, as defined in 24

# Introduction
CFR 570.200(a)(3), is to assist low - to moderate -income (LMI ) residents with at least 70% of its funding.
Within this objective, all activities must meet one or more of the three national objectives defined under 24
CFR 570.200(a)(2) as benefiting LMI families, aiding in the prevention or elimination of slums or b light,
or meeting other community development needs that have an urgency due to existing conditions that pose
a serious and immediate threat to the health or welfare of the community and where other financial resources
are not available.
HUD normally def ines a LMI area as those Census block groups with 51% or more LMI households.
However, some cities, especially younger suburban cities, have few pockets of low -income within large
block groups. As a result, HUD grants an exception when fewer than 25% of the populated block groups
contain 51% or more LMI households. In League City, to reach the 25% mark, HUD has set the LMI
threshold at 28.99%. The Main St reet /Park Ave nue Area fo r the Section 108 activities contains two block
groups that have 58.87 % and 35.04% LMI respectively , for a total 46.39% LMI, therefore qualify ing the
area for assistance under CDBG regulations.

# Statement of Community Development Objectives City of League City 2017 Section 108 Pre -Application Page 2
Since 2004 when the City of League City first became an Entitlement Jurisdiction, it has end eavored to
focus its CDBG funds on single specific areas over time to make the greatest impact. After several years
of focusing on Shellside, a neglected area in south League City, the area is no longer eligible as a low - to
moderate -income neighborhood. Now the City has turned its attention and resources to the Main
Street/Park Avenue area with the highest concentration of low - to moderate -income households and many
of the oldest residential and non -residential structures in the city. It is also an area of immense potential
for economic development, expanding small businesses and improving amenities.
The City of League City proposes to use its Section 108 loan funds to augment other funds to facilitate
reinvestment and prevent the negative effects of d isinvestment in the Main Street/Park Avenue Area. The
Main Street/Park Avenue Area is a major part of the larger Downtown Re vitalization Area. The Downtown
Revitalization Project will establish the area as a community gathering spot and help build a conne ction
among residents and business owners. The area consists of two adjoining CDBG -eligible block groups,
which comprise a single mixed use, though predominately residential, neighborhood. During the
development of the past two Consolidated Plans, the pub lic and City staff set this area as having the highest
priority need for revitalization and concentrated improvements. To date, the City has used CDBG funds to
construct Mustang Park, a public park, in partnership with Clear Creek Independent School Distr ict.
Additionally, CDBG funds are allocated annually to Interfaith Caring Ministries, located in the
neighborhood, to provide rent and utility assistance to residents at risk of eviction or losing utilities. The
City also provides CDBG funds to I nterfai th Caring Ministries for their food pantry at the same location .
Additionally, the City used CDBG -R funding to construct a sidewalk along Park Avenue to connect the
residences south of Main Street to Main Street and commercial areas north of Main Street , as well as to
provide safe pedestrian access to League City Elementary School, the new Mustang Park, Interfaith Caring

# Statement of Community Development Objectives City of League City 2017 Section 108 Pre -Application Page 2
Ministries and the new Gulf Coast Center office on Main. The City uses CDBG funds to support part of
the salaries of Communities in Scho ols counselors at three League City schools. The offices for
Communities in Schools Bay Area are located in the Main Street/Park Avenue Area.
Though not funded at this time through CDBG, Gulf Coast Center is the Galveston County’s MHMRA
agency that prov ides services, programs and employment assistance for individuals with intellectual and
developmental disabilities, mental illness, HIV, and/or substance use disorders. Gulf Coast Center also
manages Connect Transit and provides transportation from League City to medical and social service
appointments through both the League City Park & Ride and the Demand Response Service , including the
provision of ADA Paratransit Service, for the elderly and disabled. Also, south of Main Street is Helen’s
Garden which is a City public park, Clear Path Alternative School, and CCISD Technology Learning
Center. Several small businesses and churches are along both sides of Park Avenue, S. Iowa Avenue, and
Reynolds Avenue south of Main Street .
Creatorspace, located at 120 Park Avenue is also a non -profit located in the area, though is not currently
funded by CDBG. Creatorspace is a 501(c)(3) that provides classes, technical assistance, workshops, tools,
materials and work space to promote skill -building and innovation in t echnical, artistic, and scientific areas
for individual youth, adults, and entrepreneurs.
In addition to the non -profit agencies located in the area, t here are a number of local businesses a long both
sides of Main Street and Park Avenue, as well as scatte red throughout the area north of Main, particularly
in the northeast section of the area. The infrastructure improvements proposed to be funded with CDBG
and the Section 108 loan will be a major incentive to maintain existing businesses and attract new sm all
businesses to the Main Street/Park Avenue area. The area is struggling to retain existing businesses and
attract new businesses due to the deteriorating infrastructure and abandoned lots and buildings. City of League City 2017 Section 108 Pre -Application Page 3

# Statement of Community Development Objectives City of League City 2017 Section 108 Pre -Application Page 2
The area of the neighborhood north of Main Stre et includes the City’s Historic District, League Park, the
emergency services that serve the area, neighborhood churches, and local businesses. There are more than
a dozen non -residential historic properties and 30 historic homes in the area, as well as a number of century -
old oaks that are on the historic registry. It is critical that League City maintains the historic nature of the

# Introduction
The City of League City, Texas is requesting $1,591,860 in funding under the Section 108 Loan Guarantee
Program of the U.S. Departme nt of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development
Block Grant (CDBG) Program. The Section 108 Loan Guarantee Program allows CDBG Entitlement
Jurisdictions to pledge up to five years of expected CDBG funding to guarantee a loan as a source of
financing for economic development, housing rehabilitation, public facilities, and infrastructure. Cities
such as League City do not receive enough CDBG funding in any one year to allow for the completion of
large -scale physical development and rehabil itation projects. In addition, HUD regulations to not allow
Entitlement Jurisdictions to “stock -pile” their allocations over several years to build sufficient funding for
a project. Therefore, the loan guarantee program provides loans large enough to car ry out larger local
projects that can revitalize and improve neighborhoods. The loans are required to be repaid within 20 years
and to not absorb all of the annual CDBG allocation. The current and future CDBG allocations are a
security for the loan.
Se ction 108 obligations are financed through underwritten public offerings. Financing between public
offerings is provided through an interim lending facility established by HUD. Interest rates on interim
borrowing are priced at the 3 -month London Interban k Offered Rate (LIBOR) plus 20 basis points (0.2%).
As of August 16, 2016, the 3 -month LIBOR rate is 0.82%, and with the added 0.2%, the total is 1.02%.
Permanent financing is tied to yields on the U.S. Treasury securities of similar maturity to the prin cipal
amount. A small additional spread, depending on maturity, will be added to the Treasury market yield to
determine the actual interest rate.
The activities to be carried out with the Section 108 -guaranteed loan must meet HUD’s community
development objectives as well as the City’s priorities detailed in its latest PY 2017 -2021 Consolidated
Plan. The primary objective of the CDBG program and the Section 108 -guaranteed loan, as defined in 24
texts.5:
# Introduction
CFR 570.200(a)(3), is to assist low - to moderate -income (LMI ) residents with at least 70% of its funding.
Within this objective, all activities must meet one or more of the three national objectives defined under 24
CFR 570.200(a)(2) as benefiting LMI families, aiding in the prevention or elimination of slums or b light,
or meeting other community development needs that have an urgency due to existing conditions that pose
a serious and immediate threat to the health or welfare of the community and where other financial resources
are not available.
HUD normally def ines a LMI area as those Census block groups with 51% or more LMI households.
However, some cities, especially younger suburban cities, have few pockets of low -income within large
block groups. As a result, HUD grants an exception when fewer than 25% of the populated block groups
contain 51% or more LMI households. In League City, to reach the 25% mark, HUD has set the LMI
threshold at 28.99%. The Main St reet /Park Ave nue Area fo r the Section 108 activities contains two block
groups that have 58.87 % and 35.04% LMI respectively , for a total 46.39% LMI, therefore qualify ing the
area for assistance under CDBG regulations.

focus its CDBG funds on single specific areas over time to make the greatest impact. After several years

moderate -income neighborhood. Now the City has turned its attention and resources to the Main
Street/Park Avenue area with the highest concentration of low - to moderate -income households and many
of the oldest residential and non -residential structures in the city. It is also an area of immense potential

Entitlement Jurisdictions to “stock -pile” their allocations over several years to build sufficient funding for
a project. Therefore, the loan guarantee program provides loans large enough to car ry out larger local
projects that can revitalize and improve neighborhoods. The loans are required to be repaid within 20 years
and to not absorb all of the annual CDBG allocation. The current and future CDBG allocations are a
security for the loan.
Se ction 108 obligations are financed through underwritten public offerings. Financing between public
offerings is provided through an interim lending facility established by HUD. Interest rates on interim
borrowing are priced at the 3 -month London Interban k Offered Rate (LIBOR) plus 20 basis points (0.2%).
As of August 16, 2016, the 3 -month LIBOR rate is 0.82%, and with the added 0.2%, the total is 1.02%.
Permanent financing is tied to yields on the U.S. Treasury securities of similar maturity to the prin cipal
amount. A small additional spread, depending on maturity, will be added to the Treasury market yield to
determine the actual interest rate.
The activities to be carried out with the Section 108 -guaranteed loan must meet HUD’s community
development objectives as well as the City’s priorities detailed in its latest PY 2017 -2021 Consolidated
Plan. The primary objective of the CDBG program and the Section 108 -guaranteed loan, as defined in 24

CFR 570.200(a)(3), is to assist low - to moderate -income (LMI ) residents with at least 70% of its funding.
Within this objective, all activities must meet one or more of the three national objectives defined under 24
CFR 570.200(a)(2) as benefiting LMI families, aiding in the prevention or elimination of slums or b light,
or meeting other community development needs that have an urgency due to existing conditions that pose
a serious and immediate threat to the health or welfare of the community and where other financial resources
are not available.
HUD normally def ines a LMI area as those Census block groups with 51% or more LMI households.
However, some cities, especially younger suburban cities, have few pockets of low -income within large
block groups. As a result, HUD grants an exception when fewer than 25% of the populated block groups
contain 51% or more LMI households. In League City, to reach the 25% mark, HUD has set the LMI
threshold at 28.99%. The Main St reet /Park Ave nue Area fo r the Section 108 activities contains two block
groups that have 58.87 % and 35.04% LMI respectively , for a total 46.39% LMI, therefore qualify ing the
area for assistance under CDBG regulations.
